title: Hello, Research Blog
text:
Math
A simple way to think about graph embedding is as a map \(f: V \to \mathbb{R}^d\) from nodes to vectors that preserves structural similarity. One common training objective, following the skip-gram formulation used in Grover and Leskovec (2016), is
\[
\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{u \in V} \sum_{v \in N(u)} \log \frac{\exp(f(u)^\top f(v))}{\sum_{w \in V} \exp(f(u)^\top f(w))}.
\]
Graph convolutional approaches such as Kipf and Welling (2017) instead learn embeddings by propagating and transforming neighbor features layer by layer:
\[
H^{(l+1)} = \sigma\left(\tilde{D}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \tilde{A} \tilde{D}^{-\frac{1}{2}} H^{(l)} W^{(l)}\right).
\]

An executable figure
A toy graph, laid out in 2D as a stand-in for a learned embedding:


Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx

G = nx.karate_club_graph()
pos = nx.spring_layout(G, seed=7)
colors = ["#4C72B0" if G.nodes[n]["club"] == "Mr. Hi" else "#DD8452" for n in G.nodes]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
nx.draw_networkx(G, pos, node_color=colors, edge_color="#cccccc", with_labels=False, node_size=120, ax=ax)
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()








Figure 1: Spring layout of a small random graph, used here as a toy 2D embedding.





Nodes cluster by club membership even without any learning — a reminder that a good layout algorithm and a good embedding model are solving related problems.
